body:
Awesome start - thanks for leading on this! Reading over this as a user, here are my thoughts:

Structure:

Right now it feels like we could focus / frame the narrative more around user needs.

Maybe instead of just tool node -> execute manually -> non-explicit tools, we could frame it based on what the user wants to accomplish. These approaches aren’t mutually exclusive but illustrate ways we use tool calling to accomplish different tasks.

1. ToolNode: Directly execute tool functions.
    1. When it’s useful: if you can define utilities in specific 
    2.  Routing is between two nodes (llm and tool node). End condition is if no tool calls are present. Always execute values in the tool calls of the last ai message.
2. Customize the tool node: 
    1. Routing can still be between two nodes (llm and tool node). End condition is if no tool calls are present.
    2. Can combine the LLM’s provided values with other state or custom variables. Or could stream nested inputs within a node, etc.
3. Customize Routing: 
    1. “Tools” don’t have to be single functions, they are just ways for an LLM to generate structured output that your application can use. How it uses it is up to you. Some tools may not even correspond with a single scoped “tool” - they can be used for routing or for responding in a structured format. 
    2. We could actually maybe provide two examples here:
        1. If you want your app to “remember” the previous actions it has taken: maintain the `messages` list: The agent / llm node is the same as above and returns  messages
        2. If you want complete control and don’t want your LLM to keep track of all the previous action turns as messages: The llm uses `with_structured_output` or something similar and we store that schema in the state rather than as a message

And then remind the user again that these aren’t exhaustive or mutually exclusive.




Finally,  my take on general /style points for the final draft:

- Remove unnecessary adjectives (“simple”) and adverbs (“very”, “extremely” )  - either be specific about what the user gains or what something does, or remove entirely if it’s not meant to communicate something specific.
- For built-ins like “ToolNode”, link to the reference doc (https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/reference/prebuilt/#toolnode)
- Try to avoid “lots of”  - this is intimidating to a reader. The reader needs it cleanly spelled out based on the distinct jobs they do. If there are two ways of doing something, just show one, or motivate the second example with a real need “I need to be able to combine the LLM output with other variables and so will choose to customize how I execute the tool calling a node”

I think language like this may contribute to people thinking you "have to" use langchain, etc. 

I don't have a perfect ording but all this is more like:

"Tools" are functions you've exposed to the model. Sometimes, you want to let the LLM populate only a subset of the functions' arguments; your program can provide the rest. If you're using LangChain-style tools, an easy way to handle this is by annotating function parameters with `InjectedArg`. This excludes that parameter from being shown to the LLM.

If you're using LangGraph's prebuilt ToolNode, we have a couple additional special `InejectedArg` types you can use to tell the graph to populate the tool with values from the state, store, or configuration.

```suggestion
Tools are useful whenever you want an agent to interact with external systems. External systems (e.g., APIs) often require a particular input schema or payload, rather than natural language. When we bind an API, for example, as a tool, we give the model awareness of the required input schema. The model will choose to call a tool based upon the natural language input from the user and it will return an output that adheres to the tool's required schema. 
```

```suggestion
In the ReAct architecture, an LLM is called repeatedly in a while-loop. At each step the agent decides which tools to call, and what the inputs to those tools should be. Those tools are then executed, and the outputs are fed back into the LLM as observations. The while-loop terminates when the agent decides it has enough information to solve the user request and it is not worth calling any more tools.
```
